title: 【从零开始的Godot游戏开发】#01 引擎安装与瓦片系统基础
text:
Welcome to the first episode of our 'Godot
Game Development from Scratch' series.
In this video, we'll officially kick off
development of our eight-direction shooter, 'Netherknights:
Bring It On'.
As always, all game assets are in the link
in the video description.
The tutorial will be updated, and all content is free forever.
So, without further ado,
let's start with downloading the engine.
Head to the site and grab the latest version.
For this tutorial, we're using version 4.6.1.
And while we're at it,
let's cover a question many have: version compatibility.
Godot largely follows semantic versioning,
so minor and patch versions within the same major release
are generally compatible and easy to migrate.
Only when crossing major versions, like from 3.x to 4.x,
do we need to be cautious, especially when upgrading projects.
So, even if you're watching this video
and Godot has updated to a later 4.x version,
our current tutorial content
will still be perfectly up-to-date.
At most, you'll see minor UI differences
or updated documentation descriptions,
all of which are covered in the official migration notes.
Next, we'll click 'Download,'
which takes us to the download page.
Then, click 'Godot Engine'.
This .NET version is for those
who want to use C# as their scripting language.
Considering compatibility and the learning curve
for beginners,
we'll prioritize this Godot Engine version with GDScript.
If you're interested, we can do a separate zhuan ti later on,
focusing specifically on the differences between
GDScript and C#
in scripting and project organization.
Besides the engine itself,
there's one more thing we need to download.
Scroll down the page and find 'Export templates'.
These are templates
for publishing and exporting your project,
though we won't use them right now.
But to save you the trouble of coming back to find it,
let's grab it now while we're at it.
Of course, further down,
we can also see links for getting it through Steam
and others.
Personally, I prefer this portable, no-install version.
Managing different versions is clearer.
Besides the official site,
we can also head to the Godot repo's Releases page on GitHub
for more versions and downloads.
However, for beginners,
I wouldn't recommend downloading from GitHub.
There are more versions and build options,
which can be distracting.
Of course, some of you might have trouble downloading
due to network issues.
So, in the links provided in our intro,
Besides all the game assets for this tutorial,
I've also prepared cloud drive links for the engine itself
and the export templates.
Unzip the program archive we downloaded,
and along with the template, you'll see these three files.
Double-click the program in the middle
that looks like the Godot engine icon to launch it.
The list shows the history of projects
we've opened in the past.
Next, click the 'Create' button in the top-left,
hit 'Browse' to pick a good directory,
and then type in your project name.
Keep other settings like the renderer as default,
then hit create. It'll open in the 3D View by default.
So first, let's click the 2D button
at the top of the engine to switch views.
Right now, this is still an empty scene,
so let's click the 'Create 2D Scene' button in the top-left.
First, create a root node.
You can think of nodes as small, specialized parts,
each with a job, like displaying images,
handling collisions, or sound.
A scene, then, is a reusable functional unit
formed by organizing these parts into a tree-like structure.
A character can be a scene, a bullet can be a scene,
and even the entire level can be a single scene.
Alright, let's try running this scene.
Click the triangle run button in the top-right corner,
and it'll ask us to choose which one is the main scene.
That's because during development,
we'll often create many different scenes.
The Main Menu could be one scene, the game session another,
and even different levels
might each be their own separate scene.
So, let's just select this current scene.
Since we haven't saved it yet,
it'll prompt us to choose a save location before running.
To be tidy,
we can first create a 'scenes' folder for our project.
Specifically for scene files and their corresponding scripts.
Then, rename this scene file to 'game' as well.
Here's another small detail worth mentioning:
we use lowercase for our folder and scene names,
following the snake_case convention,
with underscores separating words.
This is the best practice officially recommended by Godot.
That's because Windows and the default macOS file system
typically aren't case-sensitive.
Linux distros' filesystems are case-sensitive by default,
and Godot's exported PCK
virtual filesystem is also case-sensitive.
So if your asset naming conventions aren't consistent,
you might run into case-sensitivity issues when exporting.
Back in the project, hit 'Save,'
and we can debug in a separate window
to see how this scene looks when it's running.
Even though there's nothing on screen
yet, this small step is a giant leap into Godot development.
You've successfully set up the full pipeline
for creating, saving, and running.
Hopefully, even when you're a Godot master,
you'll still remember
this very moment—the thrill of running your first game.
Next up, importing our game assets.
After downloading the asset pack
from the link in the description,
head back to the engine interface.
Right-click and select 'Open in File Manager'
to see our project directory.
Then, copy the 'resources' folder
you got from unzipping right into here.
Inside the resources folder are three subfolders,
corresponding to the two types of game assets
we'll use: audio, fonts, and textures.
Now back in Godot, in the FileSystem panel on the left,
you can see
Godot has automatically imported these assets for us.
If we drag any texture asset into the scene window,
we'll see that in the scene node tree on the left,
Godot has automatically created a new node for us.
Now, if we zoom in on the editor
view a bit, you'll see this image starts to get really blurry.
For many beginners making a pixel game for the first time,
the reason the visuals look rough, messy, or even a bit cheap
often boils down to this.
For now, let's stick to one simple principle:
If your game's pixel art, you've gotta check first
if the textures are getting blurry from the default
smooth filtering.
First, let's make a very basic, yet crucial, setting change.
Click 'Project' in the top menu bar,
then 'Project Settings'.
On the left, find 'Rendering' > 'Textures',
and change the default texture filtering to Nearest.
You'll immediately notice
the American cockroach in the background gets super sharp.
For those without a graphics background,
the concept of texture filtering might be a bit confusing,
so let me break it down simply.
Every image is made up of countless pixels.
Right now, the asset we have is small with few pixels,
but it needs to be displayed on a much larger screen
with a greater number of pixels.
When the original and display sizes don't match,
resampling becomes needed.
Simply put, there are two main strategies:
one is Nearest Neighbor, the other is Linear.
Nearest Neighbor Filtering is straightforward:
for any given spot,
it just grabs the color from the closest pixel
and uses it directly.
So the edges stay sharp,
which fits the pixel art aesthetic better.
Linear Filtering,
on the other hand,
references nearby pixels to blend colors smoothly.
This makes the image look softer, but edges can get blurry.
So if we're using pixel art assets,
we should use Nearest Neighbor Filtering to keep them sharp.
For non-pixel art game assets,
on the other hand,
you'd typically lean towards smoothing like Linear Filtering.
Making it look more natural at different display sizes,
instead of being jagged.
Now, I'm explaining this
not so you can just memorize
which button to click in the editor,
but so you understand the 'why' behind it.
That way, next time you run into similar blurriness
in other projects,
you'll know how to diagnose it.
Alright, back in our project,
select the node we just dragged in
from the scene tree on the left side.
Press Delete or right-click to remove it.
Next up, we're diving into the actual game scene development.
To be precise, let's name
this root Node2D the same as the scene,
following the same naming convention.
However, for naming nodes within the scene,
I recommend using PascalCase,
where the first letter of each word is capitalized,
just like this example.
Develop a consistent naming style and workflow.
It might not be as quick as using default names at first,
but trust me,
it'll save you from a ton of totally avoidable headaches
down the road in development.
In the final game, you'll notice
the map behind
is actually pieced together from individual cells.
And our game assets also provide plenty of content
in the cell-style format.
So, how exactly do we use these assets in the game?
This brings us to our first key topic: the Tile System.
First, right-click on the Game node,
select 'Add Child Node,'
and then type 'Tile' into the search box up top.
You'll see two nodes with similar names
here: one is TileMapLayer,
and the other is... TileMapLayer.
Let's widen the window a bit
and check the description. You'll see
TileMap is marked deprecated,
which is the old map node version.
The official recommendation is to stop using it.
So let's go straight to TileMapLayer.
But just reading the node description,
many of you might feel a bit lost at first,
unsure where to even begin.
So, I'll take this chance
to show you all
where to find Godot's official "instruction manual."
Let's go back to the official website.
Click the 'Docs' button top-right to open the official docs,
then hit this small sidebar bottom-left
to switch the language to zh-cn Chinese.
Of course.
Due to community translation progress,
the Simplified Chinese docs
might not have every page fully translated,
but it's enough for common questions.
Next, click the search box in the top-left, and type Title.
Click 'Using TileSet' in the search results
to get to its tutorial.
Correspondingly, in the left-hand directory,
we can also find content related to TileMap.
Now, some of you might be thinking, 'Why are you showing me
the docs?
I'm watching your video *because* I can't read them!'
Hold on, we'll get hands-on with the Tile System soon.
But while we're here,
I want to quickly tell you something super important:
almost any engine-related issue...
can ultimately be found in the official docs.
A lot of beginners don't really grasp
the importance of the official docs at first.
This includes our 'Godot from Zero' tutorial series,
and pretty much all the unofficial tutorial materials
you'll find online.
Aside from the author's own experience and trade-offs,
Anything related to how the engine works,
its features, behavior, or APIs...
Their most reliable source and final stamp of correctness
almost always comes from the official docs.
The official docs are the most authoritative,
trustworthy, first-hand resource for it.
If you want to grow into a truly professional developer
who can solve problems,
then one day, you must learn to read docs.
And gradually get into the habit of checking docs.
This video series focuses on hands-on practice
with a real project,
tying together all the key concepts along the way.
Later on, we might even dive deeper
and read the Godot source code together,
which is a whole other level beyond the docs.
But at least at the start, don't be afraid of docs.
When I first started with Godot,
I'd read the docs like a novel.
Just randomly clicking pages and skimming through,
I'd often stumble upon new things in the engine.
This stuff might not be for your current project,
but it could one day, when you're tearing your hair out,
just click into place.
and suddenly spark a new solution for you.
Back to the project.
Click the 'Create' button to add a new TileMapLayer node.
To distinguish it from the decoration tile layer
later, let's just hit F2
or right-click rename and change it to GroundTileMapLayer.
Then, in the Inspector on the right,
you'll see that the Tile Set
for this tile layer is still empty.
Let's click on it and select New TileSet.
Now you'll notice that in the panel below,
two similar-looking sub-tabs have appeared,
labeled TileMap and TileSet respectively.
So, instead of digging through the docs,
let me just give you
a more precise and vivid explanation right away.
TileMap is a node for placing tiles on a 2D grid
to draw out your game world.
And TileSet is the tile resource library it uses.
It doesn't just store tile images;
you can also attach extra info to each tile,
like collision, navigation, etc.
You can think of TileSet as the paint itself,
and TileMap as our palette.
And TileMapLayer is the canvas
where we do the actual painting.
For tiles like walls, obstacles, or cracked floors,
we first need to organize them all into a TileSet resource.
Only then can we paint out the map
on the GroundTileMapLayer, tile by tile.
So back in the project, we'll start by creating a tile set.
We'll select the TileSet sub-page,
click the plus button at the bottom, and choose 'TileSet'.
Then, in the window that opens, find our static tile texture.
Double-click to select it, and it'll
ask if we want to auto-create tiles.
Just hit 'Yes'.
Now, drag this panel down a bit,
and you'll see Godot has already sliced up
the usable areas of this tile texture
into individual little cells for us.
Later, we can take these cut tiles
and start laying out the actual ground map for our game.
Now, if we click on the TileMap tab below,
we'll see that we can already select tiles
and start painting.
Let me stretch this window out a bit.
And just a quick reminder for beginners: to draw tiles,
you absolutely have to be on the TileMap page.
If you want to set the tile's properties,
you need to go back to TileSet.
Now, we can just click on any tile
and start dragging and drawing directly in the scene above.
Click the run button in the top-right,
and we'll see the tiles we just drew
appear perfectly replicated right inside the game window.
Then Ctrl+Z to undo,
and start drawing the ground map we'll actually be using.
First, we can select the rectangle tool in the bottom window,
then drag in the editor to fill a 16-by-16 map area as a base.
Next, you can freely place tiles on the map
based on your own ideas.
And that pretty much wraps up the tutorial
on how to draw with static tiles.
But if you look at our sample project,
you'll notice that quite a few tiles on the map
are actually animated.
So, how do we set up these dynamic tiles?
The process is similar.
First, let's go back to the TileSet view
in the bottom window. Click 'Add',
select our dynamic tile asset, and then hit 'Open'.
A window will pop up
asking if you want to auto-create tiles.
For now, we'll click 'No'.
We need to specify the animation frame sequence
manually later,
so we don't want it auto-cutting.
This'll give you a dim atlas
with no tile positions generated yet.
Of course, if some of you clicked 'Yes' too fast,
no worries, it's an easy fix either way.
We'll click the 'Select' button up top, marquee-
-select all the auto-generated tiles,
then just hit Delete to remove them.
Next, click 'Settings' up top to switch panels.
In the tile atlas
on the right, drag-
-select the four tile grids below the very first column.
That top row of dynamic tiles is special;
we'll deal with it separately later.
Once you've confirmed all four tiles are highlighted,
switch back to the 'Select' panel and click the first one.
Now, in the expanded animation
properties on the left, you'll see two key fields:
Speed and Mode.
Speed determines how many frames play per second.
Mode determines similar tiles.
Will they play in sync in the scene,
or randomly on their own schedules?
Synced playback looks neater, but can be a bit stiff.
Random is more dynamic,
though with too many, it might start to look disorganized.
As for the speed and mode of these four tile animations,
you can decide completely based on your own taste.
Personally, I'd slow down
the animated tiles used heavily at the borders,
so the screen isn't too busy or distracting.
As for that last tile,
the one kinda like a conveyor belt,
random playback would make the loop look unnatural.
So, I'll keep its animation mode set to Default.
Alright, the first frame's properties are set.
Next, we'll add in the rest of the animation.
Let's drag-select the four tiles again,
and expand 'Frames' on the left.
Then, click the 'Add Element' button three times,
and you'll see the subsequent tiles in the atlas
light up one by one.
This means we've successfully set up each tile
to be a four-frame animation.
Now, click the button below
to switch back to the TileMap page.
Select the first column we just set up,
and you can freely paint these dynamic tiles.
Plus, you can see their animations playing in real-time
right in the editor.
So, what about this top row of tiles?
What's that for?
First, let's take a look at the finished project.
You'll notice this row of animation
isn't actually part of the floor,
but layered on top of the ground tiles.
You can think of it as a decoration tile layer,
or an overlay tile layer.
Beneath it is the floor tile layer
we just drew a moment ago.
So, we need to head back to the editor
and first create a new tile layer.
We'll name it OverlayTileMapLayer.
Then, just like before,
create a new TileSet on the right-hand side.
Then, in the bottom window,
add the atlas and select that dynamic tile asset.
Again, click 'No' here—don't let it auto-create the tiles.
Next, under the 'Settings' panel, marquee-
-select the first frame tile we'll use.
At this point,
you'll clearly see that if you stick to the default method...
This tile, spanning two vertical cells,
will be treated as two separate tiles
instead of one single, complete tile.
So, what's the fix?
First, switch to the 'Select' panel
and delete the tile we just added.
Then, go back to 'Settings', under 'Texture Region Size',
change the Y dimension to 32.
Our base asset cells are 16 by 16 pixels,
but this decorative tile is actually 16 pixels wide by 32 tall.
So by setting Y to 32,
we can merge the two vertical cells
into one complete frame of animation.
Now, just click on the first tile again
to adjust its settings.
The rest of the steps are pretty much the same.
Switch to the 'Select' panel,
click this single lit tile,
set the animation speed to 4, and leave the mode as default.
Then, keep clicking 'Add Element' to complete the four frames.
Once that's done, use the bottom button
to go back to the TileMap page.
Select the first tile column and draw it onto the map.
Once drawing's done,
select the root node in the scene tree on the left,
and we can preview a map close to the final look.
To make sure your final result
matches our demo as closely as possible,
I've gone ahead and redrawn the tiles in full here.
Feel free to get a bit creative
when you're following along with the tutorial.
But I'd still advise
against going completely wild at this stage
and drawing a super random map.
Try to stick with our current style for now.
Because later, when we get to collision handling,
if your map layout is too random...
You'll likely run into a bunch of unique, personal problems
way ahead of time.
Now if we run the program,
we'll see the map is just crammed
into a tiny corner of the top-left, looking cramped.
Even maximizing the debug window,
the content inside doesn't actually get bigger.
Do we really have to enlarge all the tiles,
move them to the center, and redraw everything?
That would be seriously underestimating Godot.
Let me introduce you to a node you'll be using all the time
in future development:
Camera2D.
Right-click on the Game root node,
select 'Add Child Node',
search for Camera, and then add it in.
The camera concept is pretty straightforward.
Just think of Camera2D as the viewfinder
that players will ultimately see.
The scene itself can be much larger than the screen,
but what the player actually sees
is just what the camera captures.
So, our map is currently 16 by 16 tiles,
and each tile is itself 16 by 16 pixels in size.
So the actual pixel size of the entire map is 256 by 256.
If we want the map to appear
right in the center of the screen,
we can set the camera's Offset
to half of the map's total size.
Which is the position 128 by 128.
Next, if we want to make the content on screen even larger,
we'll need to adjust the Camera2D's Zoom.
Reading the tooltip on hover,
we can draw a practical conclusion right away,
inside Camera2D.
The higher the Zoom value,
the larger everything looks,
but the less you'll be able to see.
So if we want the current map to look twice as big,
we can just change Zoom to 2 and 2 directly.
With these settings applied,
running the project again shows the map centered on screen,
and the size looks much better than before.
But the overall content is still too small.
When maximized, there's a lot of empty space
around the window.
This is because the Embed Mode above defaults to 'FixedSize'.
After we select 'Keep Aspect Ratio', the issue persists.
The blank space around the window is filled.
But even so, the game content itself hasn't gotten any bigger.
Also, when we resize the window, zooming in looks fine.
But as soon as it shrinks,
only part of the screen shows,
as if it's been cropped or cut off entirely.
This brings us to a set of project settings
that are super common in 2D games.
We go to Project Settings from the top menu bar,
then find Display > Window Stretch Mode on the left.
Hovering over it shows that the default 'disabled' mode
stretches nothing,
meaning one unit in the scene
maps directly to one pixel on the screen.
This is better for non-game apps.
But if you want this project
to simply fill the entire window,
you can change it to 'canvas_items'.
Now, back in the scene, when we run it,
no matter how we resize the window,
The entire 2D view scales perfectly with the window,
so you'll never see just a small piece left on screen.
Of course, some detail-oriented folks might ask,
isn't Godot's default gray background kinda ugly?
Can we swap it
for something more flashy and extravagant black?
Of course,
and it's super easy.
Again, head to Project Settings. On the left,
find 'Rendering' > 'Environment,' then look for 'Default Clear'.
Click it, change the RGB values to 15, 15, 15,
and our background color will become a deep,
almost-black shade.
It's not just the editor's background
that changes; the game window
when you run it will be black too.
Alright, in this video, we went from having no Godot on our PC
all the way to seeing a dynamic map of our own design
in the game window.
This section focuses more on
navigating the engine editor itself.
Through these hands-on steps,
we also introduced naming conventions.
Best Practice, Texture Filtering Mode—these core dev basics.
I hope you learn not just the software operations,
but more importantly, why we do things this way
and what the principles behind it are.
We also hope that every developer interested in Godot,
after watching our tutorials,
can gradually build a mature engineering mindset
that goes beyond tutorials and truly belongs to them.
This is one of the core principles of our 'Godot
from Zero' tutorial series.
Alright, in the next video, we'll push forward,
start creating our player character,
and add extra collision rules for the map tiles.
This tutorial series will be updated regularly,
with complete content
free forever. Game assets are in the description—go grab 'em!
Thanks for liking, following, and sponsoring!
See you in the next video!

# Godot 引擎入门与瓦片系统知识图谱

## 引擎下载与版本兼容性
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A1["开始：访问 Godot 官方网站"] --> A2["下载最新 Engine（本教程使用 4.6.1）"]
    A2 --> A3["选择 .NET 版（C#）或 GDScript 版"]
    A3 --> A4["本教程优先使用 GDScript 版"]
    A2 --> A5["下载 Export Templates（稍后使用）"]
    A2 --> A6["可选：从 GitHub Releases 下载其他构建"]
    A6 --> A7["不推荐初学者使用 GitHub 版（版本过多易分心）"]
    A1 --> A8["版本兼容性说明"]
    A8 --> A9["同一主版本的 Minor / Patch 通常兼容"]
    A8 --> A10["跨主版本（如 3.x → 4.x）需谨慎迁移"]
```

## 项目创建与命名约定
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    B1["启动 Godot"] --> B2["项目历史列表"]
    B2 --> B3["点击 Create 创建新项目"]
    B3 --> B4["选择项目目录"]
    B4 --> B5["输入项目名称"]
    B5 --> B6["保持默认渲染器设置"]
    B6 --> B7["默认打开 3D 视图"]
    B7 --> B8["切换到 2D 视图"]
    B8 --> B9["点击 Create 2D Scene"]
    B9 --> B10["创建根节点（Node2D）"]
    B10 --> B11["节点类型示例：Sprite、Collision、Audio"]
    B11 --> B12["场景 = 由节点组成的可复用功能单元"]
    B12 --> B13["保存场景：在项目根目录创建 scenes 文件夹"]
    B13 --> B14["使用 snake_case 命名文件夹与场景（小写+下划线）"]
    B14 --> B15["注意：Windows/macOS 文件系统不区分大小写，Linux 区分"]
    B15 --> B16["保存后点击运行按钮"]
```

## 像素艺术纹理过滤设置
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    C1["导入资源后默认使用 Linear 过滤"] --> C2["导致像素艺术模糊"]
    C2 --> C3["打开 Project Settings"]
    C3 --> C4["导航至 Rendering > Textures"]
    C4 --> C5["将 Default Texture Filter 改为 Nearest"]
    C5 --> C6["立即看到纹理锐利（示例：美国蟑螂）"]
    C5 --> C7["解释：Nearest Neighbor 直接取最近像素颜色"]
    C5 --> C8["解释：Linear 进行颜色混合导致模糊"]
    C7 --> C9["适用于像素艺术"]
    C8 --> C10["适用于非像素艺术"]
```

## 瓦片系统工作流
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    D1["在根节点上右键 Add Child → TileMapLayer"] --> D2["重命名为 GroundTileMapLayer"]
    D2 --> D3["在 Inspector 中创建新 TileSet"]
    D3 --> D4["点击 + 选择 TileSet 子页"]
    D4 --> D5["导入静态瓦片纹理并自动切割"]
    D5 --> D6["切换到 TileMap 页进行绘制"]
    D6 --> D7["使用矩形工具绘制 16×16 基础地图"]
    D7 --> D8["完成后可在运行窗口预览"]
    D2 --> D9["添加动态瓦片：在 TileSet 中点击 Add → 选择动态瓦片资产"]
    D9 --> D10["选择 No（不自动切割）"]
    D10 --> D11["手动选中四个瓦片格子"]
    D11 --> D12["在属性面板设置 Speed 与 Mode（同步或随机）"]
    D12 --> D13["点击 Add Element 添加其余帧（共四帧）"]
    D13 --> D14["返回 TileMap 页绘制动态瓦片"]
    D14 --> D15["创建 OverlayTileMapLayer 作为装饰层"]
    D15 --> D16["在 Settings 中将 Texture Region Size Y 设为 32 以合并双高瓦片"]
    D16 --> D17["重复动画设置步骤并绘制装饰层"]
```

## Camera2D 与窗口缩放设置
